newsitem.title: USA: IMF sees Mexico real GDP growing 4.5 pct in 1997.
newsitem.headline: IMF sees Mexico real GDP growing 4.5 pct in 1997.

text.p: Mexico's real GDP should grow 4.5 percent in 1997, driven by continuing export growth and recovering domestic consumption, the International Monetary Fund said Wednesday.
"We think that exports will continue to grow relatively strongly, though we are anticipating also a significant recovery in internal demand in Mexico," said the IMF's chief economist, Michael Mussa.
Mussa spoke at a news conference held for the release of the IMF's World Economic Outlook report, ahead of next week's IMF/World Bank joint spring meeting.
Mexico's economy grew 5.1 percent last year, rebounding from a 6.2 percent contraction in 1995 due to the peso crisis.
The 1995 recession depressed real wages and consumption, which remained subdued during 1996, Mussa said.
However, he added that the IMF has already seen signs that Mexico's growth "will reflect more and more a recovery of internal demand".
In its World Economic Outlook report the IMF also said that it expected Mexican inflation to drop to about 17.3 percent from last year's 34.1 percent rate.

Regarding the peso, the report noted that the Mexican currency had stabilized late last year after it weakened six percent in October on concerns over the announcement of the 1997 economic policy program and privatizations.
The peso recovered its footing after the Mexican central bank tightened monetary policy and agreement was reached with business and labor leaders for the 1997 policy targets, the report said.
By the IMF's projections, Mexico's current account deficit is due to widen to 1.25 percent of GDP this year, after it increased slightly to 0.5 percent of GDP in 1996.
